title: Rama's sandals on the throne
hookLine: a prince sets his brother's sandals on the throne, and pilgrims still carry their saints' sandals: why Hindus bow to the feet
carry: bowing to the feet honors the one who walked first
tomorrow: A hymn that ends on perhaps
last: IN BHAKTI, THE SONG BELONGS TO GOD.

lines: A BROTHER WHO WON'T COME HOME.
cards: A prince walks into the forest to find his older brother and bring him home to be king. Rama refuses. He gave his word to their father, and he'll keep his fourteen years of exile.

So Bharata asks for one thing: Rama's sandals. In the Ramayana, Bharata carries them home on his own head, sets them on the throne, and rules in Rama's name, from a village outside the capital, until his brother returns.
Today, the last summit sit on the regions, and a pair of sandals.

teach.b: That story sits under a practice Hindus still keep: honoring the feet, and what the feet stand for. The sandals aren't Rama. They mark the road he walked, and the throne he gave up to keep his word.
In Maharashtra, the Varkaris live this every year in the rains.

teach.h: THE VARKARIS CARRY THEIR SAINTS' PADUKAS.
teach.b: Crowds of pilgrims walk to Pandharpur, singing, and at the heart of the procession, in palanquins, ride the silver padukas of their saints, Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram. Not statues. Sandals.
The saints walked this road; now the road walks with them.

teach.h: A HAND ON THE HEAD: A BLESSING.
teach.b: Across India, students honor a guru's padukas, and a child touches a grandparent's feet at a birthday or before a trip, and gets a hand on the head in return: a blessing. Many teachers put the meaning simply.
The feet carried that person through a whole life, so you honor the road they've walked and what they bring back from it.

teach.h: EACH REGION IN ITS OWN WORDS.
teach.b: The regions this year kept the same instinct in their own words.
In Kerala, a pilgrim to Sabarimala carries a two-part bundle on the head, offerings on one side and food for the road on the other, and pilgrims call one another Swami.
In Bengal, Durga comes home as Uma, a daughter, and is carried back to the river. In Kashmir, walnuts kept through Shiva's great night are shared with family and neighbors.
Each place has its own language and its own saints, and none is ranked above another.

teach.h: BOW TO THE ONE WHO WALKED FIRST.
teach.b: But the gesture at the heart of today is one of the oldest: bending low before the one who walked first.

how: Many Hindus touch the feet of parents, grandparents and teachers to ask their blessing; the Varkari pilgrimage carries the padukas of Dnyaneshwar and Tukaram to Pandharpur each year; and regional observances such as Durga Puja in Bengal, Herath in Kashmir and the Sabarimala pilgrimage in Kerala are kept in their own languages and customs.

games.q: your grandmother arrives for her birthday, and you bend to touch her feet. what are you honoring?
o: the road she's walked, and you're asking her blessing.
her rank, the way you'd bow to a queen.
games.why: like Bharata with Rama's sandals, you honor the one who walked first, and her hand on your head is the blessing back.

practice: Bring to mind an elder or teacher whose feet you've touched, or might: a grandparent, a guru, someone who walked a hard road before you. Picture bending down, and their hand resting on your head.
Stay there for a few breaths, and silently thank them for one thing they carried to you. If you pray, you can end with a pranam to God, hands together at the heart.

wordCard.voice: The summit sit. One stretch of the year, seen from the top. Today's stretch, and the last: the regional traditions, and what each place carries. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit, in Devanagari: pādukā, sandals; the ones Bharata set on the throne, and the ones the Varkaris carry.
